panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Low-power (4×) H&E of a shave biopsy from the right arm/forearm showing spongiotic-acanthotic epidermis with focal parakeratosis and a mixed lichenoid, perifollicular and perivascular infiltrate; the in-text explicitly states these coexisting spongiotic and lichenoid features are recognised histological patterns of Grover disease rather than arguments against it. B: High-power (40×) H&E showing a focal acantholytic cleft (arrow) with dyskeratotic keratinocytes (arrowheads) at a fibrinoneutrophilic exudate; the in-text identifies recurrent focal acantholysis as the key finding supporting the diagnosis of Grover disease.

(A) Spongiotic-acanthotic epidermis with focal parakeratosis and a mixed lichenoid, perifollicular and perivascular inflammatory infiltrate (original magnification 4×). (B) Focus of acantholysis (arrow) at the margin of a fibrinoneutrophilic exudate; dyskeratotic keratinocytes are indicated by arrowheads (original magnification 40×).
in_text_mentions: luent parakeratosis, a mixed inflammatory infiltrate with a lichenoid, perifollicular and perivascular distribution, small foci of acantholysis with occasional dyskeratotic keratinocytes, associated with a fibrinoneutrophilic exudate (Figure 3). Although acantholysis was focal, its recurrence in specimens obtained during a separate disease episode, in the same clinical setting as the initial biopsy, was regarded as the key finding supporting the diagnosis; the coexisting spongiotic and lichenoid features are recognised histological patterns of GD rather than arguments against it (Section 3.3).

panels.attribution_text: Maghiar et al. Chronic-Recurrent, Limb-Predominant Grover Disease in a Young Adult: A Clinicopathological Diagnostic Challenge. Diagnostics (Basel, Switzerland) 2026. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 2.

in_text_mentions: haemorrhagic crusts, were distributed predominantly over the proximal upper limbs and thighs, with only discrete truncal involvement and post-inflammatory macules on the posterior trunk (Figure 1A,B). Vesicles, bullae and pustules were absent. Dermoscopy showed a nonspecific inflammatory pattern of focal pink-red erythema, fine superficial scale and superficial haemorrhagic crusts (Figure 2). No burrows and no delta-wing jet signs were identified at any of the examined sites, and there was no involvement of the interdigital web spaces or the genital skin, findings that argued against scabies.

The caption and article text describe focal hypergranulosis and suprabasal cleft containing acantholytic and dyskeratotic keratinocytes, which are characteristic histological findings for transient acantholytic dermatosis (GD), consistent with Grover's disease.

in_text_mentions: attern. Focal hypergranulosis and suprabasal clefts containing acantholytic and dyskeratotic keratinocytes were observed in the epidermis. A loose perivascular lymphoid infiltrate, which included a few eosinophils and neutrophils, was found in the superficial dermis (Figures 2 and 3). Direct immunofluorescence was negative. During hospitalization, skin lesions began to improve. The patient was discharged to the outpatient-clinic to continue follow up. Skin lesions disappeared in two months. Clinicopathologic features were consistent with the diagnosis of transient acantholytic dermatosis (GD).
